ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Jamnagar-Loni LPG Pipeline 
* 121. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) the project cost of cross coun try LPG pipeline from Jamnagar 
(Gujarat) to Loni (U.P.) commissioned in May, 2001 by GAIL; 
(b) what is its capacity and capacity utilis ation in the last three month i.e. 
July to September, 2001; 
(c) what would be the saving in transport cost in terms of Rs./ Cu.m. and 
what impact it will have on the pricing of LPG cylinder; and 
(d) whether this impact in pricing will affect all the consumers in general 
or only the consumers of the States through which this pipeline passes? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The project cflst""of cross Gountry liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) 
pipeline from Jamnagar to Loni, which was commissioned on 31.1^2001 and 
dedicated to the Nation by the Hon'ble Prime Minister on 09.05.2001^ as Rs. 
1,229.45 crore. 
(b) The capacity of the pipeline is 1.7 million tonnes per annum 
(MMTPA) and the average capacity utilisation for the period July to 
September, 2001 was 76%, with month-wise utilization for July, August and 
September, 2001, being 69%, 75% and 83% respectively. 
(c) and (d) The current transport cost of LPG through the pipeline 
1 

RAJYA SABHA       [27 November, 2001] 
is Rs. 1.30 per metric tonne per kilometer. The estimated savings in transport 
cost would be approximately Rs. 260 crore per annum. Passing these savings 
to consumers of domestic LPG is not possible, as LPG is heavily subsidized. 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: Sir, first, I would like to compliment the hon. 
Minister for the performance shown by this pipeline, which, over these last 
few months, has an average capacity utilization of 76 per cent. In fact, in the 
month of September the capacity utilization has been 83 per cent; and it has 
been increasing. Sir, my first supplementary relates to performance not only 
on operational basis, but also on financial basis, because, for a very long time 
our public sector has been performing very well, operationally, but we have 
not had a proper return on the financial investment made. In this context, I 
would tike to know from the hon. Minister as to what has been the internal 
rate of return or pay back period norms for this project, and how does it 
compare with an international project of this size, because the annual benefit, 
as he has pointed out, is Rs. 260 crores, on an investment of more than Rs. 
1200 crores. 
SHRI RAM NAIK: Sir, as has been given in the reply, Rs. 260 
crores would be the saving in transport cost, which would mean that if the 
LPG had been brought either by tankers or by rail, the transportation coat 
would have been Rs. 260 crores more, in one year. That means, we would 
save Rs. 260 crores, in one year. In add ition to that, both in the case of rail 
and road, we use diesel; because of the pipeline, our saving on diesel, in one 
year, would be to the extent of Rs. 87 crores. So, these are the savings. As for 
the general performance, I would like to point out that out of the 232 public 
sector undertakings, all our PSUs are Navratanas or mini ra tanas. They are 
in the first top ten, so far as performance is concerned. I must also thank the 
hon. Member for the compliments that he has given. 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: Sir, I did not get an answer for my question as 
to what the IRR is, but I would be satisfied if the hon. Ministr could send that 
to me in writing. My second supplementary has to do with his clarification that 
there will be no savings to the domestic consumers of LPG because the LPG is 
already subsidised for the 
2 

[27 November, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA 
domestic consumers. I would like to request the hon. Minister, if he 
could enumerate some of the qualitative benefits of the project, 
particularly for the five States through which the pipeline passes 
through, in terms of how much improvement will there be in the 
 supply of LPG, or in jobs being available in these States. I mean, the 
qualitative benefits of the network. 
SHRI RAM NAIK: Sir, the most important qualitative difference would be 
that there would not be any congestion on the major roads because of the gas 
tankers. So, pollution would also be reduced. Then, if we take into account 
the cost, if I carry the gas by pipeline my expenditure is Rs. 1.30 per Km. 
When it is carried by rail, it costs Rs. 2.20, which means 170 per cent more. 
When I carry it by road, it costs Rs. 3.02 per kilometre, which means 230 per 
cent more. So, this is the financial benefit. Secondly, there would be no 
pollution and less accidents because of the gas tankers. There would be no 
adulteration. Of course, in gas also, some adulteration takes place. But when 
it comes by pipeline, there is no adultera tion. These are some of the benefits 
which will accrue because of the pipeline. 
SHRI S. VIDUTHALAI VIRUMBI: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the hon. Minister 
has just explained, through his reply, that the Government is able to save, 
approximately, Rs. 260 crores per annum by utilizing the pipeline. I want to 
know from the hon. Minister whether this utilization is as per the 
international standards or not. If it is not, whether the Government has any 
proposal to enhance the capacity utiliza tion, as per international standards 
and, thereby, would it be able to increase the savings? 
SHRI RAM NAIK: Sir, I do not have the international utilization 
standards with me just now. But I can, certainly, say that our utilization can 
be compared with the international standards, and I would like to add here 
that in September, the utilization was 83 per cent. Now that the winter has 
set in, the consumption will increase. So, by December or January, we might 
increase the utilization to 95 per cent or even 100 per cent, because the 
people would require more gas, and we would be in a position to provide 
that. So, the utilization percentage would also increase in these months.

houses of Gujarat being starved of gas? Why arc you not giving gas as per

Joint venture fields which were given to joint-venture private companies

Now, about the reduction in the gas supplied to Gujarat. Sir, whatever gas

SHRI RAM NAIK: Sir, in the case of gas, commitments are always made

factories are built. As we are exploring the gas, in expectation of the gas 
which is likely to come, commitments are made. Sometimes even the power 
plants are also delayed. So, based on that, the system of supplying the gas 
has been developed. There are two asp ects to it. One is the committed and 
the other is the fallback. Fall-back gas is also given. On the basis of how 
much gas is available, we are distributing it. Of course, commitment is there, 
but actual distribution is made on the basis of the availability of gas.

State Government.

Jharkhand 
(i) 2.36 lakh hac. annual irrigation in East & West Singhbum districts.

(iii) Power-8 mw

(i) 1.14 lakh hac. irrigation. 
(ii) Flood control benefits, (to Orissa also)

* 132. PROF. A. LAKSHMISAGAR: 
SHRI H. K. JAVARE GOWDA: 
Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the fatigued and strained pilots are being 
forced to fly the Indian Airlines flights thereby endangering the safety of 
passengers; 
(b) if so, what are the reasons therefor; and 
(c) what action has been taken by Government to check such practices? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SYED SHAHNAWAZ 
HUSSAIN): (a) No, Sir. International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) 
requires that the State of the operator establish regulations specifying the 
limitations applicable to the flight time and flight duty periods for Flying Crew 
members. These regulations also make provision for adequate rest periods 
and shall be such as to ensure that fatigue occurring either in flight or 
successive flight or accumulated over a period of time due to this and other 
tasks, does not endanger flight safety. Accordingly, the Director General of 
Civil Aviation (DGCA) has laid down the Flight and Duty Time Limitations 
(FDTL) as also for rest period s, and these are binding on all

Benefits under WTO Agreements 
945. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) the stated position of India in regard to WTO agreements entered so 
far; 
(b) the details of benefits these agreements have brought to India in terms 
of greater export market access in the developed west particularly in 
Textiles, agriculture exports; 
(c) whether it is a fact that WTO regime is not enthusiastic about cross 
border movement of labour which is not only India's key concern but 
considered component of trade in services; and 
(d) if so, whether Indian delegation attending WTO Conference at Doha 
recently expressed our concern on such matters? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) India is founding 
member of WTO and strongly favours the strengthening of the rule-based 
multilateral trading system of the WTO which came into existence in 1995. 
However, in the course of implementation of WTO Agreements over the last 
6 years, there is clear perception of 'development deficit'. The inherent 
imbalances in the WTO agreements, the non-operationalisation of the Special 
and Differential Treatment Clauses in favour of developing countries and the 
lack of sincere implementation of their obligation by developed countries are 
apparent. India along with other like minded Member countries have 
highlighted these "implementation related issued concerns" in WTO. 
79 

RAJYA SABHA       [27 November, 2001] 
(b) WTO provides a predictable non-discriminatory rule based 
multilateral trading system. By virtue of being a member of WTO, 
India is automatically entitled to get Most Favoured Nation (MFN) 
and National Treatment from all other members, for its exports. 
Specifically, the Agreement on Agriculture (AoA) mandates 
disciplines on market access, domestic  supports and export subsidies. 
As per WTO statistics India's share in world exports of agriculture 
commodities, which stood at 1.3% for the period 1991—94, increased 
to 1.9% for the year 1998. In the context of textiles, the provisions of 
the Agreement on Textiles and Clothing (ATC) mandate eventual 
integration into GATT of Trade in the area of Textiles and Clothing 
by 2005, after which the multilateral trading rules of GATT/WTO 
would be applicable. The integration is being carried out in four 
stages over the 10 ( ten)-year transition period. So far, various 
countries have integrated into GATT 1994 Textiles and Clothing 
Products, which accounted for not less  than 33% of th e total volume 
of country's 1990 imports of the products in this area. In accordance 
with the provisions of ATC, WT O members countries have also 
notified their schedule for integrating the further 18% of the total 
volume of 1990 import of the products in this area, to be effective 
• from January 2002. The process of integration into GATT 1994 of trade in 
this area have so far not resulted in any meaningful removal of quotas in 
respect of developing countries as the integration process is backloaded and 
restraining members have chosen to integrate mainly those products which 
are not under quota. Indian exports in textiles and clothing sectors increased 
from Rs. 285203 million in 1995-96 to Rs. 552424 million in 2000-01. 
(c) The General Agreement on Tr ade in Services (GATS) under 
WTO envisages four modes of delivery of Services. Modc-4 relates to 
cross border movement of natural persons. There is considerable 
asymmetry in the commitments between different modes of delivery 
in services with minimum level commitments having been taken by 
developed countries in mode 4 which is of primary interest to India 
and other developing countries. India has already submitted a 
proposal on the liberalisation of movement of professionals in the 
special sessions of the Council fo r Trade in Services (CTS). The 
Fourth 
80 

[27 November, 2001]      RAJYA SABHA 
Ministerial Conference of WTO held recently at Doha from 9th—14th 
November 2001 recognise the proposals relating to the movement of natural 
persons among various others in the context of the on-going negotiations on 
trade in services. 
(d) The Indian delegation at the Doha  Conference expressed its concerns 
on various issues including agriculture, textiles and services. On the 
agricultural negotiations, India called for elimination of large-scale domestic 
support and trade distorting subsidies by developed countries and removal of 
all unfair barriers to farm exports from developing countries. At the same 
time, India stressed that our concerns relating to food and livelihood security 
and rural development are adequately ta ken care of. Similarly in services, it 
was pointed out that facilitating the movement of professionals must receive 
priority attention. India also exhort ed the WTO membership at Doha to 
make sincere efforts in resolving the outstanding implementation related 
issues and concerns or giving clear directions on how to deal with them.

food security and livelihood concerns and has, inter-alia, sought sufficient

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRA- 
VARTY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) to (d) Flood Management being a State subject, flood control schemes 
are planned, funded and executed by the State Governments themselves out 
of their own resources and as per their own priorities. Central Government 
renders assistance that are technical, catalytical and promotional in nature. 
The Government of India has set up Ganga Flood Control Commission to 
tackle the flood problem in Ganga basin, which has prepared comprehensive 
plans for flood management for all the 23 river systems of Ganga basin. 
Similarly, the Brahmaputra Board set up by the Government of India under 
an Act of Parliament has prepared Master Plan for main Brahmaputra & 
Barak valley inter-alia to control floods in North Eastern region. These plans 
have been forwarded to respective State Governments for preparing detailed 
schemes based on ground surveys and for implementation. 
The Central Government has also set up 159 Flood Forecasting Stations on 
major interstate rivers which give timely warning to all flood affected 
regions in various States. 
The Government of India constituted several expert committees to study 
the problem of floods in the country. The Rashtriya Barh Ayog (RBA) set up 
in 1976 examined the problem in detail and submitted its report in 1980. The 
recommendations of RBA, which form the framework for flood management 
strategy in the country, were forwarded to all the State Governments for 
implementation.

SHRI W. ANGOU SINGH (Manipur): Mr.  Vice-Chairman. Sir, before I 
come to the Statutory Resolution moved by the hon. Home Minister regarding 
the extension of President's rule in t he State of Manipur fo r another period of 
six months, I want to say something abo ut the situation now prevailing in the 
State of Manipur. Sir, we all know t hat Manipur was a sovereign State on 15* 
August, 1947. From that time, Manipur had its own Government, under the 
Manipur State Constitution Act, 1947. This Act was extended to the whole of 
Manipur, including the hilly areas. But, on 15 th October, 1949, an Agreement 
was signed between the Maharaja of Manipur and the Government of India. In 
that Agreement, Article 8,  Schedule III is the main problem. That has created 
the present situation in the St ate of Manipur. I want to read out that Article. It 
says, "The Government of India undertakes to make suitable provision for 
employment of the people of Manipur in the various branches of public 
services, and in every way encourage Manipuri people to join them. They also 
undertake to preserve various laws, customs and conditions prevailing in the 
State, pertaining to the social, economic and the religious life of the people." 
Here, in this Agreement, there are two Issues. These two issues are the main 
reasons for the prevailing law and order situation in the State. 
These two issues, namely, suitable provisions for employment, and 
State's economy, are the two main Issu es concerning the younger generation. 
The insurgent groups of the State c an eastty mislead the younger generation 
on these two issues. I had raised this issue in this House on a number of 
occasions, and the Government of India had replied that there was a mention 
of suitable provision for employment In the Agreement. They had given the 
reply that it had already be en fulfilled. Now, the sit uation is that, in Manipur, 
nearly 60 per cent of the population bel ong to the Hindu Meitel community, 
and the remaining are Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. Now, the 
Government of India has reserved a ce rtain percentage for the employment 
of* Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. But as far as the majority Hindu 
Meitel Community Is concerned, the Go vernment has not taken any specific 
measure. Because of this, the Hindu Me itei Community is not getting proper 
employment opportunities. The Government of India should, at least, take 
some specific measures so that t he Hindu Meitel Community can compete 
with others for appointment in public services. The present Government and 
the previous government have done nothing in this direction. This is my first 
point.

RAJYA SABHA [27 November, 2001] 
there was no indication of Greater  Nagaland, which has been over-
emphasised; it was more from the la w and order angle that it was done.

[THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in the Chair)

SHRI C. APOK JAMIR: I would not like to take much time of the

[27 November, 2001] RAJYA SABHA

SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA : Ma dam Deputy Chairman, while

SOME HON. MEMBERS: He did not say like that. 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Okay. It was a peculiar impasse

RAJYA SABHA [27 November, 2001] 
Madam, what I would like to say is that, it was the extreme 
insensitivity of the Governments, or the rulers and the administrators, be they the

of October, 1949, and, for 23 years, it was under Central rule. I am indebted to 
Shri Shourie for reminding the House that there were 17 Governments; and 7 
times, President's rule was promulgated, without effecting any change in the life of 
the common Manipuris, Manipuris are facing a serious problem of unemployment. 
There is no industrialisation. There is no development. I think non-development is 
a perennial problem in the North-East, as a whole, and in Manipur in particular. No 
honest attempts have been made to effect development programmes In Manipur, 
either by the State Governments or by the Central Government. First of all, it is this 
extreme in sensitivity of the administration which has to be taken care of. 
When there was a mass upsurge against the extension of the 
agreement with the NSCN (IM), I was in Manipur, along with the Left M.Ps., on

monetarily or by any other means; I am sorry to say, Madam, that the 
insensitivity of the administration still persists in Manipur. The problem of 
unemployment Is menacing in Manipur. No positive attempt, no well-meaning 
attempt, has been made to solve the problems of Manipur. It Is a fact when the 
Governor 
256 

[27 November, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
tells the delegation-Mr. Arun Shourie also referred to it—that in Manipur, 
unfortunately, the Government is a Gove rnment by the bureaucrats, of the

principals. Only six regular principals are running 44 higher secondary

Kumar Sharma, the Secretary of the Co uncil of Higher Secondary Education, 
was involved in marks tampering scandals in respect of his own wards. The

that because personally I know that Mr. Ved Marwah is a very able

I am just telling you about the si tuation of the intelligentsia of

257 

RAJYA SABHA [27 November, 2001] 
salary of Rs.2000 per month and nothing extra is being paid to them. There is

{Time Bell) Madam, the problem is so enormous, the problem is so horrendous

folk in Manipur. But that project has been halted by the Government of India. Dr. 
Shourie should take special interests in such things, where the indigenous 
production of silk can be guaranteed by such projects. But these 
 
258

[27 November. 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
projects are not being looked into property. I will say that it is a situation where 
the Government has been insensitive inso far as the economic plunder of the 
State is concerned, insofar as co rruption is concerned, insofar as

situation will change. The people must have the confidence that the 
259 

RAJYA SABHA [27 November, 2001] 
Government of India and the people of India are sensitive to their problems. Unless

able to change the situation.

different, let the hon. Home Minister not say that the Manipur elections can be held 
along with the elections in Punjab and Uttar Pradesh. Since the Manipur situation

like to suggest that the Manipur situation should be properly supervised and seen

development are to be initiated. Development means what touches the sensitivity of 
the people. That must be ensured. With  these words, I support the Resolution 
moved by Shri LK. Advani, subject to the observations that I have made.   
Thank you. 
SHRI SHANKAR ROY CHOWDHURY : Madam Deputy Chairperson, 
it is a matter of happiness for me that a Statutory Resolution should have resulted

placed in charge and

the Governor's rule, the economic projects which have been sanctioned, must
